title: Security & Compliance: RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency, SDLC, Incident Response, Evidence Workflows, and Risk Exceptions
author: Maya Chen
body:
Summary

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's security and compliance controls and operational procedures across the following domains: RBAC and authentication, audit logging, data residency and retention, secure SDLC expectations, incident response security procedures, compliance evidence workflows, and risk & exceptions handling. It is intended for engineering, platform, security, and compliance stakeholders responsible for design, implementation, and evidence generation.

Scope and audience

- Scope: All Redwood-managed hosted services, Dedicated and Private deployments (control plane and data plane), and supporting infra (CI/CD, SSO, logging stacks, key management).
- Audience: Service owners, platform engineers, SRE, security, compliance, product, and SOC.

Principles and goals

1. Principle of least privilege: RBAC should grant minimal permissions required for job function.
2. Immutable, auditable evidence: All control actions affecting production must be logged and retained according to policy.
3. Data locality and contractual compliance: Customer data residency controls must be enforced and demonstrable.
4. Secure-by-default SDLC: CI/CD pipelines and build artifacts must enforce signing, scanning, and gated deploys.
5. Fast, secure incident handling: Security incidents must follow a documented playbook with evidence capture and post-incident remediation tracking.

1) RBAC and Authentication

Overview
- Primary identity provider: Okta for Redwood-hosted control plane and corporate SSO.
- Service accounts: Managed through AWS IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) on EKS or equivalent in other cloud providers.
- Customer identities (for Private deployments): Option to integrate customer IdP via SAML/OIDC; documented mapping required.

RBAC model
- Global roles: admin, security-admin, platform-engineer, svc-account, read-only, support-agent.
- Resource-scoped roles: model-catalog-admin, deployment-operator, monitoring-viewer, billing-viewer.
- Role assignment rules: use groups in Okta; group-to-role mapping maintained in the identity-management repo (ownership: platform).

Controls and enforcement
- Privileged access requires 2FA (Okta MFA) and device posture (Intune/Jamf compliance for corp endpoints).
- All changes to role definitions require a PR in identity-management repo and CI validation.
- Time-bound admin elevation: use ephemeral sessions via Bastion/Just-In-Time access (JIT) with approval recorded in access-requests service.

Operational checks and SLOs
- Weekly audit: owner_team must review active privileged principals (SLO: 100% weekly scans, auto-flag stale accounts >30 days).
- Orphaned key detection: automated run every 24h, remediation within 72h.

Example: Creating a service role for a new microservice
1. Define least-privilege IAM policy in identity-management repo (YAML).
2. Open PR and tag platform and security reviewers.
3. After approval, CI deploys role and updates central RBAC registry.

2) Audit logging

Goals
- Capture who/what/when/where for all control plane and sensitive data plane actions.
- Ensure log integrity and availability to security and compliance teams.

Logging sources and pipeline
- Sources: API gateway (request/response metadata), control plane services (create/update/delete of models, deployments, rollouts), infra actions (terraform apply, KMS use), authentication events (Okta), admin console actions (Console UI, CLI).
- Pipeline: Fluentd/Vector -> Kafka -> Splunk / Datadog SaaS or customer-provided SIEM (for Dedicated/Private) -> Long-term archive in write-once S3 bucket with lock.

Retention and integrity
- Default ingestion retention (hot): 90 days in Splunk/Datadog for operational use.
- Compliance retention: configurable per-customer policy; minimum for regulatory customers: 7 years.
- Integrity: logs are hashed on ingestion, with periodic snapshot hashes stored in KMS-protected manifests. Tamper-evidence checks run weekly.

SLOs and thresholds
- Log ingestion latency: 95th percentile < 30s for control plane events.
- Audit export success rate: 99.9% per day for scheduled archival jobs.

Example Audit Event (JSON snippet)
```
{"timestamp":"2026-11-02T14:22:31Z","actor":"okta:users/12345","action":"deployment.create","resource":"deployments/rdx-prod-42","result":"success","ip":"203.0.113.44","trace_id":"trace-abc-123"}
```

3) Data Residency and Retention

Policy summary
- Customer data is tagged with a residency label at creation time (region: us-east-1, eu-west-1, ap-southeast-1).
- Hosted plan customers may select region constraints; Dedicated/Private customers can enforce on-prem or VPC-local storage.
- Cross-region replication is prohibited unless explicitly requested and contracted.

Retention matrix (high-level)
| Data class | Default retention | Compliance minimum | Storage class |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Control plane logs | 2 years | 7 years (regulated) | S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval |
| Audit logs | 90 days (hot) / archive 7 years | 7 years | S3 + Glacier |
| Model artifacts (non-customer) | 1 year | N/A | S3 Standard |
| Customer model data / embeddings | customer-configurable | customer-contract | Customer-managed KMS + regional S3 |
| Backups (db snapshots) | 30 days | 7 years (if in contract) | Encrypted S3 |

Data handling and enforcement
- Residency is enforced by the deployment controller: provisioning of storage and compute is region-locked.
- Automated pre-deploy policy checks block deployments that would place customer data outside allowed regions.
- Data deletion requests: follow the Data Subject Request (DSR) runbook (see Appendix). Deletion must remove primary and replicated copies and generate a deletion certificate.

4) Secure SDLC (software supply chain controls)

Requirements (applies to all services touching customer data)
- All commits must be linked to a ticket and have signed commits for release branches.
- Static analysis: Snyk/Checkov/Trivy scans in CI with gating thresholds (no critical or high with exploitability score >7 allowed).
- Dependency policies: auto-upgrade bot + weekly dependency review; disallowed packages enumerated in dependency-blocklist.
- Build provenance: every released artifact must include SBOM and provenance metadata; artifacts are stored in signed, versioned repositories (Artifactory/GitHub Packages).
- Secret scanning: prevent commits containing secrets; block PRs via pre-merge CI checks.

Release process
1. Feature branch -> PR with tests and security checklist ticked.
2. CI runs tests, static scans, SCA, and SBOM generation.
3. Signed build is created; signature stored in keyring (HSM-managed).
4. Canary rollout to Dedicated pool, monitor security and performance metrics for 48h.
5. Gradual rollout to global pool with automatic rollback on security regression or integrity failure.

5) Incident response - security procedures

Classification and SLAs
- Incident severity levels: Sev-1 (active data exfiltration/production compromise), Sev-2 (service compromise with limited blast radius), Sev-3 (suspicious activity, failed intrusion attempt).
- Initial detection to Triage: 30 minutes (goal). Incident Commander assigned within 60 minutes for Sev-1/Sev-2.

Immediate response checklist (example for suspected data exfiltration)
1. Detect and contain: isolate affected hosts, revoke compromised keys/sessions (IAM revoke + rotate KMS keys if required), and apply WAF/IP blocks.
2. Preserve evidence: snapshot instances (forensic mode), export relevant audit logs (store in secure evidence bucket with immutability).
3. Notify: security, legal, CTO, and customer-success per the escalation matrix.
4. Triage and root cause analysis: use endpoints, logs, and network flow captures.
5. Remediation: patch, rotate secrets, revoke tokens, and reissue keys; follow post-incident hardening checklist.
6. Communication: draft customer notification (if required) and regulatory notifications (72-hour GDPR timeline if personal data breach).
7. Post-incident review: 2-week remediation tracking with owners and verification.

Evidence capture and chain-of-custody
- All artifacts collected during incident response must be cataloged in the incident ticket and stored in an immutable S3 prefix with access limited to SOC and security leadership.
- Hashes and collection timestamps recorded and signed by incident lead.

6) Compliance evidence workflows

Standard evidence packages
- Controls mapping: mapping from control IDs to evidence artifacts (e.g., CIS, SOC2 CC, ISO27001). Control-to-evidence mapping stored in compliance-repo (owner: security/compliance).
- Evidence types: configuration snapshots, access reviews, audit log extracts, SBOMs, build signatures, penetration test reports, policy documents, change approvals.

Evidence generation cadence and responsibilities
- Quarterly: access reviews, vulnerability scan summaries, penetration-test status.
- Monthly: control health dashboard export, system configuration snapshots for production.
- On-demand: evidence package for customer audits within 7 business days (standard SLA). Extended requests may have commercial terms.

Packaging and delivery
1. Create evidence collection task in compliance-repo.
2. Pull artifacts using automated evidence tooling (governance-runbook CLI).
3. Validate artifacts against control checklist.
4. Produce signed package and deliver via secure transfer (pre-authenticated S3 URL or secure portal).

Example governance-runbook commands
```
# export access review for tenant-123
gov-runbook export-access --tenant tenant-123 --since 2026-08-01 --out tenant-123-access-review.json
# package signed artifact
gov-runbook sign-artifact --artifact tenant-123-access-review.json --key hsm://projects/redwood/keys/prod-signing
```

7) Risk and exceptions

Accepted risk model
- Risks are tracked in the risk register with associated compensating controls and acceptance period (max 12 months unless exceptional approval).
- Minor exceptions (low-impact) can be approved by service owner + security reviewer; major exceptions require security leadership and legal sign-off.

Exception process (5-step)
1. Submit exception request with risk assessment and compensating controls.
2. Security performs review and assigns risk rating (Low/Medium/High).
3. Mitigation plan and timeline agreed; short-term compensating controls implemented immediately.
4. Approvals recorded in risk-register (Git-backed) with reviewer signatures.
5. Re-evaluate before expiry; extension requires re-approval.

Example: Temporary cross-region replication request
- Owner must demonstrate encryption-in-transit + rest, customer consent, and update contract. Exception TTL: 90 days; required controls: IP allowlist, enhanced monitoring, daily audit export.

Roles and ownership (summary)
- Security (owner): policy definition, audit evidence, incident leadership, risk approvals.
- Platform (owner): RBAC enforcement, deployment controller checks, identity-management repo.
- Eng SRE (owner): logging pipeline, ingestion SLOs, archive jobs.
- Product (owner): customer-facing residency options and contract terms.
- Legal/Compliance (owner): contractual requirements, regulatory notifications, audit liaison.

Appendix A - Example configurations and command snippets

1) Example Fluentd to Kafka snippet (for prod control plane events)
```
<match redwood.controlplane.**>
  @type kafka_buffered
  brokers kafka-prod-1:9092,kafka-prod-2:9092
  topic controlplane-audit
  flush_interval 5s
</match>
```

2) Retention policy Enforcement Pseudo-Rule (Pre-deploy)
```
if resource.data_region != tenant.allowed_region:
  fail("Data residency check failed: target region not allowed")
```

Appendix B - DSR (Data Subject Request) deletion checklist
- Verify identity and authorization.
- Locate all primary and replica copies (storage, backups, analytics buckets).
- Execute deletion, run verification jobs, and produce deletion certificate with hashes and timestamps.
